q: Name a disease of humans that is caused by a protist.

pts.a: Malaria (caused by Plasmodium), or amoebic dysentery, or sleeping sickness

right: Malaria, which is caused by the protist Plasmodium
wrong: Tuberculosis (TB)
Athlete's foot
Measles
why: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a single-celled protist that a mosquito passes into the blood. TB is caused by a bacterium, athlete's foot by a fungus and measles by a virus.

q: Tapeworms are parasitic animals that live in the human intestine. State how a person usually becomes infected with a tapeworm.

pts.a: By eating raw or undercooked meat (pork, beef or fish) that contains tapeworm larvae (cysts)
accept: eating raw meat with tapeworm cysts in it
eating meat that is not cooked properly

right: By eating raw or undercooked meat that contains tapeworm larvae
wrong: By being bitten by an infected mosquito
By breathing in droplets when an infected person coughs
By touching an infected person's skin
why: Tapeworm larvae live in the muscle of infected pigs, cattle or fish. Eating that meat raw or undercooked lets them reach the gut, so cooking meat thoroughly prevents it.

q: Name a disease of humans that is caused by a fungus.

pts.a: Athlete's foot, or ringworm, or thrush

right: Athlete's foot
wrong: Tuberculosis (TB)
Malaria
The common cold
why: Athlete's foot is caused by a fungus that grows on warm, damp skin between the toes. TB is caused by a bacterium, malaria by a protist and the common cold by a virus.

q: Ringworm is a skin infection of humans and animals. What type of organism causes ringworm?

pts.a: A fungus

right: It is caused by a fungus
wrong: A parasitic worm that lives in the skin
A bacterium
A virus
why: Despite its name, ringworm is not a worm: it is a fungus that grows outwards through the skin, leaving a red ring. It is treated with antifungal cream.

q: State the role of natural killer (NK) cells in the body.

pts.a: They destroy body cells infected by viruses, and cancer (tumour) cells

right: They destroy body cells that are infected by viruses, and cancer cells
wrong: They make antibodies against one specific antigen
They engulf and digest bacteria by phagocytosis
They remember an antigen so that a second attack is beaten fast
why: NK cells are white blood cells that recognise body cells that are infected with a virus, or cancerous, and make them die. Antibodies come from B cells, and engulfing is done by phagocytes.

q: Natural killer (NK) cells are part of the innate (general) immune system. Explain why.

pts.a: They are non-specific: they attack any infected cell without needing to recognise a particular antigen
accept: they do not target one specific antigen

right: They attack any infected cell: they are not specific to one antigen
wrong: They make antibodies that fit one particular antigen
They only attack a pathogen they have met before
They form memory cells after an infection
why: The innate system is always ready and is not specific: NK cells act on any virus-infected or cancer cell at once, without needing to learn one antigen or making memory cells.

q: What is meant by the cell-mediated immune response?

pts.a: T lymphocytes (killer T cells) attack and destroy infected body cells directly, without antibodies
accept: killer T cells destroy infected cells
T cells kill body cells infected by a virus
T cells attack infected cells themselves

right: Killer T cells attack and destroy infected body cells directly
wrong: B lymphocytes make antibodies that bind to antigens in the blood
Phagocytes engulf any pathogen they meet
Memory cells give long-term protection against an antigen
why: In the cell-mediated response the T cells themselves do the work: killer T cells bind to body cells that show viral antigens and burst them with perforin. No antibodies are involved.

q: What is meant by the antibody (humoral) immune response?

pts.a: B lymphocytes make antibodies, which lock onto the antigens of pathogens in the blood and body fluids
accept: plasma cells make antibodies against the antigen

right: B lymphocytes make antibodies that lock onto antigens on the pathogen
wrong: Killer T cells release perforin to burst infected cells
Phagocytes engulf pathogens and digest them with enzymes
Suppressor T cells switch off the immune response
why: In the humoral response B lymphocytes make antibodies that float in the blood and lymph and bind to antigens on free pathogens, marking them for phagocytes to destroy.

q: Distinguish between the roles of B lymphocytes and killer T cells in the immune response to a virus.

pts.a: B lymphocytes make antibodies against the virus (the antibody or humoral response)
accept: B cells give the humoral response

pts.a: Killer T cells destroy the body cells that are infected with the virus (the cell-mediated response)
accept: killer T cells kill infected cells
T cells destroy infected body cells
T cells give the cell-mediated response

right: B cells make antibodies; killer T cells destroy the infected body cells
wrong: Both make antibodies that bind to the virus
B cells engulf viruses; T cells make memory cells
B cells make antibodies; T cells engulf and digest the virus
why: Antibodies from B cells deal with viruses outside cells. Once a virus is inside a cell, antibodies can't reach it, so killer T cells destroy the infected cell itself.

q: Give one example of a disease of humans that is caused by an RNA virus.

pts.a: Influenza (flu), AIDS (HIV), COVID-19, measles, mumps, polio or the common cold

right: Influenza (the flu)
wrong: Chickenpox
Cold sores (herpes)
Tuberculosis (TB)
why: Flu viruses carry their genes as RNA. Chickenpox and cold sores are caused by DNA viruses (herpes viruses), and TB is caused by a bacterium.

q: The flu virus is an RNA virus. Explain why a new flu vaccine is needed every year.

pts.a: RNA viruses such as flu mutate quickly (often), because errors are made copying their RNA
accept: it has a high rate of mutation

pts.a: So new strains appear with different antigens, which antibodies and memory cells from last year's vaccine don't recognise
accept: memory cells do not recognise the new virus

right: Its RNA mutates quickly, so new strains appear with different antigens
wrong: The antibodies made by the vaccine only last for one year
The flu virus becomes resistant to the vaccine
Memory cells are all destroyed every winter
why: RNA is copied with more mistakes than DNA, so flu mutates fast. New strains have changed antigens that last year's memory cells don't fit, so the vaccine is updated each year.

q: A disease has a reproduction number (R value) of 3. What does this mean?

pts.a: On average, each infected person passes the disease on to 3 other people
accept: each case infects three other people
every infected person passes it on to 3 people
each person infects 3 others on average

right: Each infected person passes it on to 3 other people, on average
wrong: 3 people in every 100 have the disease
An infected person stays ill for 3 weeks
The disease kills 3% of the people who catch it
why: R is the average number of people each infected person passes the disease on to. With R = 3, 1 case leads to 3, then 9, then 27: the outbreak grows fast.

q: What happens to the number of cases of a disease when its R value stays below 1? Explain why.

pts.a: The number of cases falls and the outbreak dies out
Each infected person passes it on to fewer than one other person on average
accept: each person infects less than one other person
each case causes under one new case

right: Cases fall, as each infected person infects less than one other on average
wrong: Cases rise, because each person infects more than one other
Cases stay the same, as each person infects exactly one other
Cases fall, because the virus mutates into a weaker strain
why: If each case causes less than one new case, every round of infection is smaller than the last, so the outbreak shrinks and dies out. Above 1, each round is bigger and it grows.

q: What is meant by a carrier of an infectious disease?

pts.a: A person who is infected with the pathogen and can pass it on, but has no symptoms
accept: someone who has the pathogen but shows no symptoms
a person infected without feeling ill
a person who is not ill but can spread it

right: A person who has the pathogen and can pass it on, but has no symptoms
wrong: An animal, such as a mosquito, that carries a pathogen between people
A person who is in hospital with the disease
A person who is immune because they had the disease before
why: A carrier is infected and can spread the pathogen but is not ill, so nobody knows to keep away. An animal like a mosquito that carries a pathogen is called a vector.

q: Some people carry a pathogen for years without feeling ill. Explain how this helps the disease to spread.

pts.a: They don't know they are infected, so they don't stay away from others or take precautions
accept: they are unaware they have it
they do not know they are infected

pts.a: The pathogen persists in them, so they can infect others over a long period
accept: the pathogen persists in their body
they can infect people for a long time

right: They don't know they are infected, so they keep passing it on for a long time
wrong: Their immune system is stronger than other people's
The pathogen mutates inside them into a deadly strain
They take antibiotics, which kill the pathogen
why: A carrier has no symptoms, so they mix freely instead of staying away from others, and because the pathogen persists in them they can infect people for months or years.

q: Give one example of chemical resistance, apart from antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

pts.a: Insecticide (pesticide) resistance in insects, fungicide resistance in fungi, herbicide resistance in weeds, or antiviral resistance in viruses

right: Mosquitoes becoming resistant to the insecticides used to kill them
wrong: Bacteria becoming resistant to penicillin
Viruses becoming resistant to antibiotics
People becoming immune to measles after a vaccine
why: Any chemical that kills a pest or pathogen selects for resistant mutants: insecticides in mosquitoes, fungicides in fungi, herbicides in weeds and antivirals in viruses.

q: A farmer sprays the same insecticide every year and it stops working. Explain how the insects became resistant to it.

pts.a: A few insects had a mutation (variation) that made them resistant
accept: a mutation made some insects resistant
some insects had a variation that made them resistant

pts.a: The resistant ones survived the spray and reproduced, passing the resistance gene on to their offspring
accept: the resistant insects survived and reproduced
they passed on the resistance gene

right: A few had a mutation for resistance; they survived the spray and reproduced
wrong: The insects got used to the spray and built up immunity to it
The spray caused mutations in every insect that made them resistant
The insects made antibodies against the insecticide
why: The spray doesn't cause resistance: it kills the insects without the resistance mutation. The few resistant ones survive, breed and pass on the gene, so the population becomes resistant.

q: State one way in which the movement of people can help an infectious disease to spread.

pts.a: Infected people (who may have no symptoms yet) carry the pathogen to new places or countries, where others catch it
accept: travellers bring the pathogen to new countries
infected people carry it to other areas
air travel spreads it around the world quickly

right: Infected people carry the pathogen to new countries, where others catch it
wrong: People who travel build up immunity to every disease
Moving about makes the pathogen mutate faster
Pathogens die when they are moved to a different climate
why: People travel far and fast, often before symptoms show, so an infected traveller can bring a pathogen to a place where nobody is immune and start a new outbreak there.

q: Ash dieback is a fungal disease of ash trees. Explain how importing young ash plants from abroad could bring the disease into a new country.

pts.a: The imported plants (or the soil with them) may already be infected, carrying the fungus or its spores
accept: the imported plants are already infected

pts.a: The fungus then spreads to the native ash trees, which have no resistance to it
accept: the native trees have no resistance
local ash trees are not resistant to it

right: They carry fungal spores that spread to native ash with no resistance
wrong: The imported plants are weaker, so they die and rot
The ash trees mutate when they are moved to a new climate
Insects from abroad eat the leaves of the trees
why: Young plants can look healthy while carrying the fungus. Once planted, its spores blow onto native ash trees, which have never met the disease and so have no resistance to it.

q: What is meant by a novel virus?

pts.a: A new virus that has not been seen before in that species, often one that has jumped from animals to humans
accept: a virus never seen before in humans
a virus that has jumped from animals to humans

right: A new virus that has never been seen before in that species
wrong: A virus that mutates very quickly, like the flu
A virus that only infects bacteria
A virus that contains DNA instead of RNA
why: A novel virus is new to a species, often after it spills over from animals, as SARS-CoV-2 did. Nobody has immunity to it, so it can spread fast.

q: Name one novel virus that has spread from animals into humans.

pts.a: SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), bird flu, swine flu or MERS

right: SARS-CoV-2, the coronavirus that causes COVID-19
wrong: The common cold virus
Measles
Tuberculosis (TB)
why: SARS-CoV-2 is closely related to bat coronaviruses and first spread in humans in 2019. Measles and colds have been in people for centuries, and TB is a bacterium, not a virus.

q: Explain why it is important for society to know about emerging diseases.

pts.a: So they can be found and controlled early, before an epidemic or pandemic, and vaccines and treatments developed in time
accept: so the spread can be controlled
so vaccines can be developed in time
to be prepared for an outbreak

right: So outbreaks are found and controlled early, before they become a pandemic
wrong: So that people never catch any disease again
So that antibiotics can be given to everyone with a virus
So that doctors know which bacteria cause the common cold
why: A new disease caught early can be contained by testing and isolation, and work on vaccines and treatments can start, before it becomes an epidemic or a pandemic.

q: What is meant by an autoimmune disease?

pts.a: A disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own cells (it treats self as foreign)
accept: the immune system attacks the body's own tissues
the body's own cells are treated as foreign
when your antibodies attack your own body

right: A disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own cells
wrong: A disease caused by a virus that attacks the immune system, such as HIV
An allergy: the immune system overreacts to harmless pollen
A disease the body can cure by itself without medicine
why: Normally lymphocytes ignore the body's own antigens. In an autoimmune disease they treat self as foreign and attack it, e.g. the insulin-making cells in type 1 diabetes.

q: Name one autoimmune disease.

pts.a: Type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, coeliac disease or lupus

right: Type 1 diabetes
wrong: Type 2 diabetes
AIDS, caused by HIV
Hay fever
why: In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys the pancreas cells that make insulin. Type 2 diabetes is not autoimmune, AIDS is caused by a virus and hay fever is an allergy.

q: In type 1 diabetes, which cells of the body are attacked by the immune system?

pts.a: The insulin-making (beta) cells of the pancreas (in the islets of Langerhans)

right: The cells in the pancreas that make insulin
wrong: The liver cells that store glucose as glycogen
The red blood cells that carry glucose
The cells of the small intestine that absorb glucose
why: Lymphocytes destroy the beta cells in the islets of the pancreas, so little or no insulin is made and blood glucose stays too high. People with it need insulin injections.

q: Apart from vaccines and medicines, give two ways to control the spread of a new infectious disease.

pts.a: Isolating infected people (quarantine)
Contact tracing
accept: tracing the contacts of infected people

pts.a: Testing and surveillance to find cases early
Controlling vectors such as mosquitoes (nets, repellent, draining standing water)
Wearing masks (face coverings)
Good hygiene: washing hands, disinfecting surfaces
Social distancing (avoiding crowds)
Limiting travel (border controls, lockdown)

right: Isolating infected people and tracing their contacts
wrong: Isolating infected people and giving everyone antibiotics
Eating a healthy diet and getting plenty of sleep
Keeping warm and drinking plenty of fluids
why: Isolation stops infected people passing it on, and contact tracing finds the people they met before they spread it. Antibiotics are a medicine, and a good diet won't stop the spread.

q: What is meant by contact tracing?

pts.a: Finding the people an infected person has been in close contact with, so they can be tested or isolated
accept: identifying everyone an infected person has met
finding the people who were in contact with a case

right: Finding everyone an infected person has met, so they can be tested or isolated
wrong: Testing everyone in the country for the disease
Keeping infected people away from everyone else
Tracking where the mosquitoes that carry the virus breed
why: Contact tracing finds the people an infected person has been near, so they can be tested and isolated before they pass it on. That breaks the chain of spread.

q: What type of medicine is used to treat athlete's foot?

pts.a: An antifungal (cream, powder or drug)

right: An antifungal cream
wrong: An antibiotic cream
An antiviral drug
A vaccine
why: Athlete's foot is caused by a fungus, so it needs an antifungal, which kills fungi or stops them growing. Antibiotics act on bacteria, and antivirals on viruses.

q: Antiviral drugs are used to treat some viral infections. State one way an antiviral drug can work.

pts.a: It stops the virus copying itself (replicating) inside the host cell, or stops it entering or leaving cells
accept: it stops the virus from replicating
it blocks the virus entering host cells
it prevents new viruses being released

right: It stops the virus from copying itself inside the host cell
wrong: It kills the virus by breaking down its cell wall
It makes the body produce antibodies against the virus
It stops bacteria from making their cell walls
why: Viruses multiply inside our own cells, so antivirals target virus-only steps: getting into cells, copying viral genes or releasing new viruses.
